title: Think of Christ as of God
sum: The sermon begins without a greeting. The preacher tells his 'brothers' to think of Jesus Christ 'as we think of God, as the Judge of the living and the dead', because whoever thinks little of Christ hopes for little. Then he reminds them where they came from: they had bowed down to images made by human hands, their life was 'nothing but death', and their eyes were full of mist. Christ took pity on them, gave them light, called them sons, and brought them into being 'out of nothing'.
Two questions run through the chapter: what can we give him in return (1:3, 5), and do we know what we were saved from? The rest of the sermon answers the first: confess him by what you do.

views.H: The chapter gives the one firm fact about the first hearers: they were Gentile converts from idol worship (1:6). Lightfoot used it to argue that the writer is not Clement of Rome, who writes in 1 Clement as an heir of Israel.
views.N: 'The Judge of the living and the dead' is the phrase of Acts 10:42, 2 Timothy 4:1 and 1 Peter 4:5. Light given to the blind, life to the dead and calling 'out of nothing' are Paul's pictures of salvation (2 Corinthians 4:6; Romans 4:17).
views.P: A sermon that starts not with a text but with a demand: take Christ seriously, and remember what you were. Gratitude is the motive of everything that follows.

echoes: Acts 10:42; 2 Timothy 4:1; 1 Peter 4:5; Psalm 115:4-8; 1 Thessalonians 1:9; Romans 4:17; 2 Maccabees 7:28; Hebrews 6:4

settings.what: Opening of the sermon: Christ, the hearers' past, and the barren woman
settings.by: An unnamed preacher, who later says he is reading his sermon aloud (19:1)
settings.to: His 'brothers' in a Christian congregation, Gentiles who had once worshiped idols (1:6)
settings.when: At a meeting for worship, after the reading of Scripture (19:1); the date is uncertain, Lake's 'between 120 and 170 A.D.', most often about 150
settings.why: To make the hearers take Christ and their salvation seriously before he asks anything of them: remembering how much he gave and what they were saved from is the ground of the whole appeal.
settings.readers: Christians who had once 'bowed down to stones and wood, gold, silver and bronze' (1:6), so Gentile converts, gathered for worship. Lake gives three views of where they lived: Rome (Harnack), Corinth (Lightfoot) or Alexandria (other scholars).
views: Harnack: the letter that Soter, overseer of Rome about 166-174, sent to Corinth, for which he probably used an old homily (Lake's report).
Lightfoot: a homily preached at Corinth and kept there beside 1 Clement, which is why the two were later copied together.
Other scholars, Lake reports, regard the external evidence as 'practically valueless' and see an Alexandrian homily, from its theology and its possible use of the Gospel of the Egyptians.

deep.h: A sermon with a high view of Christ
deep.b: Lake sums up the sermon's aim in three phrases: 'to inculcate a high Christology, a pure life, and a belief in the resurrection of the flesh.' The first stands in the opening sentence. The preacher does not argue that Christ is to be thought of 'as of God'; he assumes his hearers agree, and draws a moral from it. Later he can introduce a saying of Jesus with 'God says' (13:4), call Christ 'spirit at first' who 'became flesh' (9:5), and speak of 'the day God will appear' (12:1) where the New Testament speaks of Christ's appearing. Lightfoot noted the same habit and used it in dating the sermon.

title: The barren woman and her children
sum: The preacher reads Isaiah 54:1 in the Greek Bible's words, the same words Paul quotes in Galatians 4:27, and explains it line by line. The barren woman is 'our church', which had no children until the Gentiles believed; 'cry aloud' means pray with a single heart; the desolate woman's many children are the believers, now more than 'those who seemed to have God'. Then he quotes a saying of Jesus as 'another Scripture': 'I did not come to call righteous people. I came to call sinners.'
Lightfoot called the work 'the first example of a Christian homily', and here we watch a homily work: a verse is read, and each phrase is explained in turn.

views.H: The phrase 'another Scripture' (2:4), applied to words found in Matthew and Mark, matters for the history of the canon: George Reid called it the first use of 'Scripture' for a New Testament book after 2 Peter 3:16.
views.N: The quotation of Isaiah 54:1 agrees word for word with Galatians 4:27, and the saying of 2:4 with Matthew 9:13 and Mark 2:17. Luke 19:10 stands behind 2:7.
views.P: The preacher's method is the one preachers still use: take a text and explain it phrase by phrase ('When he said ... he meant'), then apply it to the hearers ('he meant us').

echoes: Isaiah 54:1; Galatians 4:27; Matthew 9:13; Mark 2:17; Luke 5:32; Luke 19:10; 2 Peter 3:16

settings.what: Isaiah 54:1 read and explained
settings.by: The preacher, quoting Isaiah in the Greek Bible
settings.why: To show the hearers that the prophet spoke of them: their church, once without children, now outnumbers the people who 'seemed to have God'. The verse that comforted exiles in Babylon is read as a word to a young Gentile church.
settings.readers: A Gentile church (1:6) that saw itself as the barren woman of Isaiah 54 made fruitful.

settings.what: A saying of Jesus introduced as 'another Scripture'
settings.by: The preacher, quoting the Lord
settings.why: To show that Christ came for the perishing, and so for these hearers, who were 'already perishing' (2:7).
settings.readers: Hearers who knew sayings of Jesus as part of what was read and quoted in their church.

deep.b: The preacher has just quoted Isaiah. He goes on: 'And another Scripture also says', and quotes words that stand in Matthew 9:13 and Mark 2:17. George Reid, in the Catholic Encyclopedia, called it the place where 'we find, for the first time after 2 Peter 3:16, the word Scripture applied to a New Testament book.' Lightfoot compared the Epistle of Barnabas, which introduces 'many called, but few chosen' with 'it is written' (Epistle of Barnabas 4:14), and Polycarp's Latin letter, which calls a verse of Ephesians 'Scripture' (Polycarp to the Philippians 12:1). The preacher never names a Gospel. He quotes the Lord's sayings freely, some in forms close to Matthew and Luke, some in no Gospel at all (4:5; 5:2-4; 8:5; 12:2), so whether he means a written book here is not certain.

title: Confess him, do not deny him
sum: Christ has shown great mercy: the hearers no longer sacrifice to dead gods, and through him they know 'the Father of truth'. Knowing the Father means not denying the Son. The Lord said, 'Whoever confesses me in front of people, I will confess him in front of my Father.' But how is he confessed? Not with the lips only, as Isaiah warned, but by doing what he says, with the whole heart and the whole mind.

views.N: The saying of 3:2 is close to Matthew 10:32 and Luke 12:8; Isaiah 29:13 is quoted in the short form of Matthew 15:8 and Mark 7:6, but with the verb of 1 Clement 15:2; 'whole heart and whole mind' comes from the great commandment (Mark 12:30).
views.P: The chapter turns confession from a word into a life. The question 'how do we confess him?' sets up the list of deeds in 4:3.

echoes: Matthew 10:32; Luke 12:8; Isaiah 29:13; Matthew 15:8; Mark 7:6; Mark 12:30; 1 John 2:23; 1 Clement 15:2

settings.what: Confessing Christ by deeds
settings.by: The preacher, with sayings of the Lord and of Isaiah
settings.why: To show that the gratitude owed to Christ (1:3) is paid by confessing him, and that confession means obedience, not words. The warning is meant for people who called Jesus 'Lord' but did not live by his commandments.
settings.readers: Converts from paganism for whom refusing to sacrifice to the gods (3:1) was already a public act of confession.

title: Not everyone who says "Lord, Lord"
sum: Calling Christ 'Lord' does not save. The preacher quotes a saying close to Matthew 7:21, then lists the deeds that confess him: love one another, no adultery, no slander, no jealousy; be self-controlled, merciful and good; feel one another's pain; do not love money. Fear God more than people. Then a saying of the Lord found in no Gospel: even those held 'in my embrace' will be thrown out if they do not keep the commandments.

views.H: Lake's note on 4:5: the saying's source 'is unknown: it is often supposed to have been the Gospel of the Egyptians, but there is no clear evidence of this.'
views.N: 4:2 differs from Matthew 7:21 ('will be saved' for 'will get into the kingdom'); 4:5 ends close to Luke 13:27 and Matthew 7:23 but begins with words no Gospel has.
views.P: The list of 4:3 is the sermon's plainest ethics, and its first word is the one the preacher will later say his whole sermon was about: self-control (15:1).

echoes: Matthew 7:21-23; Luke 6:46; Luke 13:25-27; Acts 5:29; Galatians 5:22-23

settings.what: A saying of the Lord in no Gospel
settings.by: The Lord, as the preacher quotes him
settings.to: Disciples who are close to him but do not keep his commandments
settings.when: Quoted in the sermon; its original setting is unknown
settings.why: To warn that closeness to Jesus is no protection for those who disobey him.
settings.readers: The congregation, who were to hear themselves in the words 'gathered with me'.

title: Lambs among wolves
sum: The hearers are resident aliens in this world, and should not be afraid to leave it. The preacher quotes a conversation between Jesus and Peter that no Gospel records: 'You will be like lambs surrounded by wolves.' 'But what if the wolves tear the lambs to pieces?' Jesus answers that dead lambs need not fear wolves; fear the one who has authority after death to throw soul and body into the fire of Gehenna. Life in this flesh is short; Christ's promise is rest in the kingdom. So treat the world's goods as someone else's.

views.H: The dialogue with Peter is one of the sermon's sayings with no Gospel source; Lake's margin marks it 'Ev. Aegypt.', but his note says there is 'no clear evidence' that it comes from the Gospel of the Egyptians.
views.N: Luke 10:3 and Matthew 10:16 (lambs, sheep and wolves) and Luke 12:4-5 and Matthew 10:28 (fear the one who can cast into Gehenna) are joined into a scene with Peter's question.
views.P: The chapter speaks to fear: fear of persecution, and the pull of the world's goods. The answer is to see the world as a foreign city and life in it as a short stay.

echoes: Luke 10:3; Matthew 10:16; Matthew 10:28; Luke 12:4-5; 1 Peter 1:17; 1 Peter 2:11; Hebrews 11:13; Matthew 11:28

settings.what: Resident aliens in this world
settings.by: The preacher
settings.why: To free the hearers from fear of those who kill and from desire for this world's goods, by reminding them that their stay here is brief and their home is the kingdom.
settings.readers: A church that could expect hostility (the wolves) and was tempted by wealth (5:6-7; 6:1).

settings.what: A dialogue of Jesus and Peter in no Gospel
settings.by: Jesus and Peter, as the preacher quotes them
settings.to: Peter, and through him the disciples
settings.when: Quoted in the sermon; its setting is unknown, though the first words recall Jesus sending out his disciples (Luke 10:3)
settings.why: To answer the disciples' fear of being killed: only God has power after death.
settings.readers: The congregation, who were to see themselves as the lambs.

title: Two ages, two masters
sum: No household slave can serve two masters, and no one can be the friend of this age and the age to come, because the two are enemies. This age calls for adultery, corruption, love of money and deceit; the other says goodbye to them. If even Noah, Job and Daniel could not rescue their children by their righteousness, what confidence can we have of entering God's palace if we do not keep our baptism pure? Who will plead for us without holy and righteous works?

views.N: 6:1 is word for word the Greek of Luke 16:13; 6:2 is close to Matthew 16:26 and its parallels; 'eternal punishment' (6:7) is the phrase of Matthew 25:46.
views.P: The first of the sermon's three calls to keep baptism pure (6:9; 7:6; 8:6). It assumes every hearer is baptized and that baptism must be guarded by the life that follows.

echoes: Luke 16:13; Matthew 6:24; Matthew 16:26; Mark 8:36; James 4:4; Ezekiel 14:14-20; Matthew 25:46; 1 John 2:1; Matthew 22:11-13

settings.what: The two ages and the purity of baptism
settings.by: The preacher, quoting the Lord and Ezekiel
settings.why: To force a choice: the hearers cannot hold on to this world's values and the age to come together, and no one else's righteousness can save them.
settings.readers: Baptized believers living in a city whose way of life the preacher sums up as adultery, corruption, love of money and deceit.

title: The contest and the crown
sum: The preacher turns to the games. Many sail in to compete for prizes that perish, but only those who train hard and compete well are crowned. In our contest that does not perish, all of us may be crowned; and if not all, let us at least come close. A cheater at the games is whipped and thrown out of the stadium. What will happen to someone who cheats in the contest of incorruption? Of those who have not kept the seal, Isaiah says, 'Their worm will not die.'

views.H: Lightfoot took the crowds who 'sail in' without any port being named as a sign that the sermon was preached near the Isthmian games at Corinth; Lake reports this as part of Lightfoot's case for a Corinthian origin.
views.N: Paul's picture of the race and the crown that does not fade, written to Corinth (1 Corinthians 9:24-27); Isaiah 66:24 in the Greek, as in Mark 9:48.
views.P: The athletic picture makes holiness a discipline to be trained for, not a feeling. 'The seal' (7:6) is baptism, which the hearers must keep unbroken.

echoes: 1 Corinthians 9:24-27; 2 Timothy 4:7-8; James 1:12; 1 Peter 5:4; Isaiah 66:24; Mark 9:48

settings.what: The picture of the games
settings.by: The preacher
settings.why: To make the hearers see the Christian life as a contest worth more effort than the athletes give, and to warn that breaking the rules of this contest, by not keeping baptism, brings a worse fate than the stadium's whip.
settings.readers: People who knew the great games at first hand. If Lightfoot is right, the Isthmian games near Corinth.

deep.b: Lightfoot's argument for Corinth rests largely on this chapter. The preacher says only that 'many sail in' (katapleousin) for the contests, without naming the place, as a speaker might do near the harbor where the competitors landed; elsewhere, Lightfoot thought, we should expect 'to the Isthmus' or 'to Corinth'. He cites Livy for the Isthmian games as a meeting place of the world 'per duo diversa maria', between two seas, and recalls that Paul's own picture of the perishable and imperishable crown was written to the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 9:25). Lake reports the view and sets it beside Harnack's (Rome) and an Alexandrian view; he does not decide. The words fit any city where people knew the games, but they fit Corinth best.

title: Clay in the potter's hand
sum: While we are on earth, let us repent. We are clay in the craftsman's hand: a potter can reshape a pot that is bent or cracked, but once it has gone into the kiln, he can do nothing more. After we leave this world, we can no longer confess or repent. So keep the flesh pure and the seal spotless. The Lord says in the gospel, 'If you did not keep what is small, who will give you what is great?'

views.N: Jeremiah 18 and Romans 9 give the potter; the saying of 8:5 joins words in no Gospel to Luke 16:10, which the preacher quotes exactly.
views.P: The kiln is the sermon's most memorable picture of urgency. It answers no question about what happens after death except one: repentance must begin before it.
views.H: 'In the gospel' (8:5) uses the word for a book or message quoted, though whether it means a written book is not certain.

echoes: Jeremiah 18:1-6; Romans 9:20-21; Hebrews 9:27; Luke 16:10-12; Luke 16:26

settings.what: Repent while there is time
settings.by: The preacher, quoting the Lord "in the gospel"
settings.why: To make the hearers repent now, by showing that death fixes a life as the kiln fixes a pot.
settings.readers: Baptized believers who had sinned after baptism and needed to be told that repentance was still open to them in this life.

title: This flesh will rise
sum: Some say this flesh is not judged and does not rise. The preacher answers: you were saved and received your sight in this flesh; you were called in the flesh, and you will come to judgment in it. If Christ, who was spirit at first, became flesh to call us, we too will receive our reward in this flesh. So guard the flesh as God's temple, love one another, and while there is time to be healed, give God what he asks: repentance from a sincere heart and praise from the heart.

views.H: Lightfoot thought the denial of the resurrection of the flesh was the false teaching the preacher 'especially dwells' on, an early form of what later became Gnostic teaching.
views.N: The argument from the incarnation to the resurrection of the body matches John 1:14 and 1 Corinthians 15; the body as temple is 1 Corinthians 6:19.
views.P: The chapter ties belief to behavior: if the body will rise and be judged, what we do in it matters.

echoes: 1 Corinthians 15:12; 1 Corinthians 6:19; John 1:14; 2 Timothy 2:18; Exodus 15:26; Matthew 12:50

settings.what: Against those who deny the resurrection of the flesh
settings.by: The preacher
settings.to: The congregation, some of whom said the flesh does not rise (9:1)
settings.why: To answer a teaching present in the church itself ('let none of you say'), and to draw from the resurrection a reason to keep the body pure.
settings.readers: A congregation where teachers were 'teaching evil to innocent souls' (10:5), probably about the body.

deep.b: 9:5 is the sermon's one direct statement about who Christ was before he was born: 'he was spirit at first and became flesh'. The manuscripts disagree on two words. Lightfoot reports that A, C, the Syriac version and Timotheus of Alexandria read 'one Christ' (heis), and only Syriac extracts 'if Christ' (ei), which he and Lake print as 'evidently required by the context'. C reads 'Word' (logos) for 'spirit', which brings the verse into line with John 1:14. Lightfoot calls the passage the pre-existence of the Son 'presented in a somewhat unusual form', and compares the Shepherd of Hermas, which calls the Son 'that Spirit'. The preacher himself uses the verse only to prove that the flesh matters.

title: Run after goodness
sum: Let us do the Father's will, run after goodness and run away from godlessness; if we pursue good, peace will pursue us. But some people bring in human fears and choose the pleasure here over the promise to come, not knowing the torment that pleasure brings. Worse, some keep on teaching evil to innocent souls, and they and their hearers will face a double judgment.

views.H: 10:3 is the sermon's most damaged verse: Lake thinks a line may have dropped out early in the copying, and Lightfoot's correction ('prosper') is a guess.
views.P: The chapter names the false teachers for the first time and judges them more harshly for leading others. It is a warning to listeners, too: 'those who listen to them' share the judgment.

echoes: Psalm 34:14; 1 Peter 3:11; James 3:1; Matthew 18:6

settings.what: Pleasure, fear and false teachers
settings.by: The preacher
settings.why: To warn hearers against teachers who make the present more attractive than the promise, and against listening to them.
settings.readers: A church with teachers in it whom the preacher considered dangerous, though he does not name them or their teaching.

title: Do not be double-minded
sum: Serve God with a clean heart and believe his promise. The preacher quotes 'the prophetic word' that 1 Clement 23 also quotes: miserable are the double-minded who say, 'We heard these things long ago, and nothing has happened.' Look at a vine: leaves fall, a shoot comes, then a sour grape, then a ripe cluster. So too my people will receive the good things after their troubles. The one who promised is trustworthy, and those who do what is right will receive what no eye has seen.

views.N: Hebrews 10:23 is quoted word for word (11:6), and 1 Corinthians 2:9 with ear before eye (11:7). James 1:8 gives 'double-minded'.
views.H: The 'prophetic word' is in no Bible. Its ending in 11:4 is not in 1 Clement, which led Lake to think both drew on the same lost book, not one on the other.
views.P: A word for a church tired of waiting for Christ's coming: the promise ripens slowly, like fruit.

echoes: 1 Clement 23:3-5; 2 Peter 3:3-4; James 1:8; Hebrews 10:23; 1 Corinthians 2:9; Isaiah 64:4

settings.what: The 'prophetic word' about the double-minded
settings.by: An unknown prophetic book, quoted by the preacher
settings.to: Doubters who said the promises had not come true
settings.why: To answer the complaint that the Lord's coming had been promised for generations and had not happened.
settings.readers: A church of the second generation or later, who had heard the promises 'in our fathers' days'.

title: When the two are one
sum: Watch for God's kingdom every hour. The preacher quotes the Lord's answer when someone asked when the kingdom would come: 'When the two are one, and the outside is like the inside, and the male with the female is neither male nor female.' He explains each line: the two are one when we speak the truth and share one soul; the outside is the body and the inside the soul, which should show in good works; and a brother and sister should not think of each other as male and female. Do this, and the Father's kingdom will come.

views.H: Clement of Alexandria quotes nearly the same saying from the Gospel of the Egyptians (Stromata 3.13). Codex Alexandrinus breaks off in 12:5, so the rest of the sermon rests on one Greek manuscript and the Syriac.
views.N: The saying is in no Gospel of the New Testament; Galatians 3:28 ('no male and female') is close in words, not in sense.
views.P: The preacher turns a mysterious saying into three practical rules: honesty, good works, purity between men and women.

echoes: Galatians 3:28; Matthew 24:36; Acts 4:32; Matthew 22:30

settings.what: A saying of the Lord on when the kingdom will come
settings.by: The Lord, as the preacher quotes him
settings.to: 'Someone' who asked him when his kingdom would come
settings.when: Quoted in the sermon; in Clement of Alexandria's report (Lightfoot prints the Greek) the questioner is Salome
settings.why: To teach that the kingdom comes as believers live in truth, good works and purity.
settings.readers: A congregation of 'brothers and sisters' (19:1) for whom purity between men and women was a live concern.

deep.h: The saying and the Gospel of the Egyptians
deep.b: Lake: 'The same saying, or very nearly so, is quoted from Cassianus by Clement of Alexandria (Strom. iii. 13), and the latter states that it is from the Gospel of the Egyptians.' In the Greek of the Stromata, as Lightfoot prints it, Cassianus gives the Lord's answer to Salome: 'When you trample on the garment of shame, and when the two become one, and the male with the female is neither male nor female.' Clement answers: 'In the four Gospels handed down to us we do not have the saying, but in the one according to the Egyptians.' Cassianus used it against marriage; Clement, in the Ante-Nicene Fathers (which gives the passage in Latin), explains the male as anger and the female as desire. The preacher of 2 Clement has no 'garment of shame', and reads the words morally. Lake adds that Grenfell and Hunt's 'Lost Gospel' from Oxyrhynchus (vol. iv) 'seems to refer to a similar saying'. Lightfoot believed the preacher used the Gospel of the Egyptians 'as authoritative', which Lake treats as uncertain for 4:5 and 5:2-4. See the topic page on sayings of Jesus outside the Gospels.

In 12:5 Lake prints the footnote 'From this point A is wanting'. The fifth-century Codex Alexandrinus, a Greek Bible now in the British Library (Fenlon's article, editor's note), contained 1 and 2 Clement with the books of the Bible; Fenlon's article on the codex in the Catholic Encyclopedia says that 'probably two' leaves are lost at the end of 2 Clement. Until Bryennios found the Constantinople manuscript in 1875, the rest of the sermon was unknown in Greek; Lightfoot speaks of 'the newly recovered ending'. From 12:5 to 20:5 the Greek rests on that one manuscript, written by Leo the Notary in 1056, and on the Syriac version, known from one manuscript of 1169 in Cambridge (Lake).

title: The name insulted among the Gentiles
sum: Repent now at last, the preacher says, and do not live only to please yourselves. The name of God is insulted among the Gentiles because of us. When outsiders hear God's sayings from our mouths, such as 'It is a credit to you if you love your enemies', they marvel. When they see that we do not love even those who love us, they laugh and call it all a myth.

views.N: Isaiah 52:5 in the Greek, as Paul quotes it in Romans 2:24; a saying close to Luke 6:32-35 introduced as 'God says'.
views.P: The chapter is about witness: the gap between the church's words and its life is what makes outsiders mock. It is one of the sermon's most modern-sounding passages.
views.H: The sermon gives a glimpse of how pagans heard Christian teaching: admiring the words, scorning the people.

echoes: Isaiah 52:5; Romans 2:24; Luke 6:27-35; Matthew 5:44-47; Colossians 4:5; 1 Peter 2:12

settings.what: The church before the watching Gentiles
settings.by: The preacher, quoting the Lord and Isaiah
settings.why: To make the hearers see their sins as a public matter: their lives decide whether God's name is honored or mocked among their neighbors.
settings.readers: A Christian group living among pagan neighbors who knew something of its teaching and watched its behavior.

title: The church before the sun and moon
sum: Those who do God's will belong to 'the first church, the spiritual one', created before the sun and moon; those who do not belong to the 'cave for bandits'. The living church is the body of Christ. God made the human being male and female: the male is Christ, the female the church. The Books and the apostles say the church has been there from the beginning; she was spiritual, as Jesus was, and was revealed in Christ's flesh. The flesh is the copy and the spirit the original: whoever corrupts the copy will not share in the original. So keep the flesh pure.

views.H: Lightfoot read 'the Books and the apostles' as the Old Testament and the apostles' writings, and the pre-existent church as a stage between Paul (Ephesians 1:4) and the Valentinians' heavenly 'Church'; he used both to date the sermon early.
views.N: Ephesians 1:23 ('his body'), Ephesians 5:32 (Christ and the church as husband and wife), Jeremiah 7:11 and Matthew 21:13, 1 Peter 1:20.
views.P: The chapter's teaching on the church serves its moral: what the believer does to his own body he does to the church, Christ's body.

echoes: Ephesians 1:4; Ephesians 1:22-23; Ephesians 5:31-32; Genesis 1:27; Jeremiah 7:11; Matthew 21:13; 1 Peter 1:20; Hebrews 9:24; 2 Corinthians 3:17

settings.what: The spiritual church and the flesh
settings.by: The preacher
settings.to: The congregation ('I do not think you are unaware')
settings.why: To give the call to keep the flesh pure its deepest reason: the believer's body belongs to the church, and the church to Christ.
settings.readers: Hearers who already knew that 'the church is the body of Christ' and could follow an argument from Scripture's 'male and female'.

deep.b: The preacher's 'first church, the spiritual one, which was created before the sun and moon' says that the church existed before the world. Lightfoot called it 'a development of the Apostolic teaching which insists on the fore-ordained purpose of God as having elected a body of men to serve Him from all eternity', citing Ephesians 1:3-4 ('he chose us in Christ before the world was founded'). He thought the phrase 'before the sun and moon' came from the Greek of Psalm 72:5 and 72:17, which, he noted, Justin read of Christ, and saw the preacher 'midway in point of development' between Paul and the Valentinians, a Gnostic school that taught an eternal heavenly being called 'Church'. For that reason he dated the sermon before Valentinus's teaching became known. The site's Galatians 4:26 ('The Jerusalem above ... is our mother') and Hebrews 12:22-23 give the New Testament's nearest pictures.

title: Advice about self-control
sum: The preacher calls his sermon 'advice about self-control'. Whoever follows it will save himself and the preacher too, for turning back a wandering soul is no small reward. The payment we owe God is to speak and listen with faith and love. Stand firm, and ask God boldly: he says, 'While you are still speaking, I will say, Look, I am here.' He is more ready to give than we are to ask.

views.P: Here the preacher names his theme and his hope. He ties his own salvation to his hearers' response (15:1), as Paul does in 1 Timothy 4:16 and James in 5:20.
views.N: Isaiah 58:9 and Isaiah 65:24 stand behind 15:3; the promise that God gives more readily than we ask recalls Matthew 7:7-11.

echoes: 1 Timothy 4:16; James 5:19-20; Isaiah 58:9; Isaiah 65:24; Matthew 7:7-11

settings.what: The preacher's own summary
settings.by: The preacher
settings.when: Near the end of the sermon
settings.why: To gather up the sermon's counsel and encourage the hearers to act on it, confident that God hears.
settings.readers: Hearers whom the preacher counts as partners: 'the one who speaks and the one who listens' (15:2).

title: The day burning like an oven
sum: While there is time and someone is ready to welcome us, let us turn back to God. The day of judgment is coming, 'burning like an oven'; some of the heavens will melt, the earth will run like lead in the fire, and every deed will be brought to light. So almsgiving is good, as repentance is; fasting is better than prayer, and almsgiving better than both. 'Love lays a cover over a great number of sins', and prayer from a good conscience rescues from death. Almsgiving lightens the weight of sin.

views.N: Malachi 4:1 and the Greek Isaiah 34:4 for the day of judgment; 1 Peter 4:8 quoted word for word; Tobit 12:8-9 behind the teaching on alms, prayer and death.
views.P: 16:4 is the verse churches have argued over most: does giving to the poor take away sin? The site's cards at Proverbs 16:6 and Tobit 4 set out the answers.
views.H: Lake's note on 'some of the heavens' points to the early Christian belief in several heavens; Lightfoot's correction reads 'the powers of heaven'.

echoes: Malachi 4:1; Isaiah 34:4; 2 Peter 3:10-12; 1 Peter 4:8; Proverbs 10:12; Tobit 12:8-9; Daniel 4:27; Matthew 6:1-18

settings.what: Judgment coming, and the works that lighten sin
settings.by: The preacher
settings.when: Near the end of the sermon
settings.why: To make the coming judgment a reason to turn to God now, and to point the hearers to the works of mercy and prayer that go with repentance.
settings.readers: A church that practiced fasting, prayer and almsgiving and needed to be told how they stood together.

deep.b: The preacher's words in 16:4 belong to a Jewish tradition that runs from Daniel 4:27 ('Break with your sins ... by showing mercy to the poor') through Tobit ('Alms rescue from death, and they cleanse away every sin', Tobit 12:9). He quotes 1 Peter 4:8 exactly, and adds a ranking no book of the Bible gives: fasting above prayer, almsgiving above both. The site gives the churches' answers in its cards at Proverbs 16:6 (where the Greek reads 'by almsgiving and faith sins are purged') and Tobit 4; this sermon, which no church counts as Scripture, adds no new card.

title: Keep the elders' warnings at home
sum: Let us repent with our whole heart, so that none of us is lost. If we must win pagans from idols, how much more must we not lose a believer. Help the weak, warn one another, and do not believe only while the elders are speaking: remember the Lord's commands at home and come more often. The Lord will gather all nations; the unbelievers will see his glory and say, 'Woe to us! It was you, and we did not know it.' Their worm will not die. The righteous, seeing the punishment of those who denied Jesus, will give glory to God.

views.H: The chapter gives the sermon's only picture of church leaders: elders who warn the congregation and announce salvation (17:3, 5). No overseer is named.
views.N: Isaiah 66:18 and 66:24 in the Greek; Philippians 2:2 ('think the same way'); Revelation 11:15 and 7:9.
views.P: A preacher's realism: people agree in church and forget at home. The cure is coming together often and holding each other to account.

echoes: Isaiah 66:18; Isaiah 66:24; Philippians 2:2; Revelation 7:9; Revelation 11:15; Wisdom of Solomon 5:1-5; James 5:19-20

settings.what: Mutual care and the final judgment
settings.by: The preacher, quoting the Lord (Isaiah 66)
settings.when: Near the end of the sermon
settings.why: To make the hearers responsible for one another and to set before them the two outcomes of the judgment.
settings.readers: A congregation led and taught by elders, meeting regularly, some of whom were weak or drifting.

title: The preacher's own confession
sum: Let us be among those who give thanks and have served God, not among the godless who are judged. Then the preacher speaks of himself: 'I myself am a sinner through and through.' He has not escaped temptation and is still surrounded by the devil's tools, but he is trying to pursue righteousness, so that he may at least come near it, because he fears the judgment to come.

views.P: The preacher puts himself under his own sermon. His 'let us' throughout is not a figure of speech only.
views.N: 1 Timothy 1:15 ('among them I am the first') and Philippians 3:12-14 (pressing on) are the nearest New Testament words.

echoes: 1 Timothy 1:15; Romans 7:18-25; Philippians 3:12-14

settings.what: The preacher's confession
settings.by: The preacher, speaking of himself
settings.when: Near the end of the sermon
settings.why: To show that his warnings come from one who needs them too, and so to make them easier to hear.
settings.readers: Hearers who were asked to repent by a preacher who confessed his own sin.

title: I am reading you an appeal
sum: Now the preacher says 'brothers and sisters' and tells what he is doing: 'after the God of truth, I am reading you an appeal to pay attention to what is written'. The reward he asks is their repentance; it will set an example for the young. Do not be angry when someone warns you, for double-mindedness and unbelief can blind us to our own wrongs. Those who obey will gather the immortal fruit of the resurrection, and the godly who suffer now will live again above with the fathers.

views.H: The verse that settles what the work is: Lake calls it 'a letter only in form', because the writer says 'that he is reading aloud' in worship. Lightfoot compared Justin's account of Sunday worship, with readings first and teaching after.
views.N: Ephesians 4:18 ('Their understanding has gone dark') is applied to the church (19:2).
views.P: A sermon read from a manuscript after the Scripture lesson, by someone Lake thinks may have belonged to an order of 'Readers'. Lightfoot called it 'the first example of a Christian homily'.

echoes: Ephesians 4:17-19; Revelation 1:3; 1 Timothy 4:13; Luke 4:16-21; 1 Corinthians 15:20

settings.what: The closing appeal
settings.by: The preacher, who calls himself 'the one who reads among you'
settings.to: 'Brothers and sisters', the whole congregation, men and women, with a word for 'the young people'
settings.when: At the end of the sermon, which followed the reading of Scripture ('after the God of truth')
settings.why: To call for repentance one last time, to prepare the hearers to accept warning, and to comfort the suffering with the hope of resurrection.
settings.readers: A worshiping congregation of men and women, young and old, for whom Scripture was read aloud and then explained.

deep.h: A sermon read after the Scripture
deep.b: 'After the God of truth, I am reading you an appeal to pay attention to what is written.' Lightfoot took 'the God of truth' as God speaking in the Scripture just read, and set the verse beside Justin Martyr's description of Christian worship: 'the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read, as long as time permits', and then the leader gives teaching and urges the hearers to follow it (First Apology 67). He thought the preacher 'was not an extempore address, but was delivered from a manuscript', and that this is why it was kept. Lake's note on 'the one who reads': 'It is probable though not quite certain that this refer to a definite order of "Readers" in the Church.' Lightfoot reports that Harnack thought the preacher a layman, because he speaks of being warned 'by the elders' (17:3); Lightfoot held that he was a church leader speaking as one of his hearers.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the reading was from Isaiah
deep.b: This is Claude's own suggestion. The sermon's Old Testament quotations lean heavily on the last part of Isaiah: it opens with Isaiah 54:1 (2:1-3), quotes Isaiah 52:5 (13:2) and Isaiah 58:9 (15:3), echoes Isaiah 34:4 (16:3), and ends its warnings with Isaiah 66:18 and 66:24 (17:4-5; already 7:6). If 'what is written' (19:1) was a reading from those chapters, the sermon would be explaining the lesson just heard, as its first chapter explains Isaiah 54:1 phrase by phrase. Lightfoot said plainly that 'we do not even know whether the lesson to which he here refers was taken from the Old or the New Testament', and the preacher also quotes many sayings of Jesus, so this remains a guess.

title: The contest of the living God
sum: Do not be troubled that the wicked grow rich while God's slaves suffer. We are competing in the trial of the living God and being trained by this life for the crown of the next. No righteous person is paid at once; if God paid right away, we would serve him for profit, not out of reverence. The sermon ends with praise to the only God who cannot be seen, the Father of truth, who sent the Savior and Founder of incorruption. Below it stands the title the manuscripts give: 'The second letter of Clement to the Corinthians'.

views.H: The closing title is the only place the name of Clement appears. Eusebius and Jerome knew a 'second epistle' and doubted it; Lake says it 'cannot have been written by the author of I. Clement'. Lake's note on 20:4 gives Harnack's view that the 'spirit' in chains is Satan.
views.N: The doxology borrows 1 Timothy 1:17, and 'Founder' is the title of Hebrews 2:10 and 12:2.
views.P: The games return (7) to frame the end: delay is training, not neglect, and it keeps faith from becoming a business.

echoes: Psalm 73:1-17; Jeremiah 12:1; Job 1:9; 1 Timothy 6:5-6; Jude 1:6; 2 Peter 2:4; 1 Timothy 1:17; Hebrews 2:10; Hebrews 12:2; 2 Timothy 1:10

settings.what: Doxology
settings.by: The preacher
settings.to: God, in the hearing of the congregation
settings.when: At the close of the sermon
settings.why: To end the appeal in praise, turning the hearers from the preacher's words to God, 'the Father of truth', whom the sermon named at 3:1.
settings.readers: The congregation, who would answer 'Amen'.

deep.h: Why the site does not call it Clement's
deep.b: The sermon names no author. The title 'of Clement to the Corinthians' comes from the manuscripts: Lightfoot reports that Codex Alexandrinus has no heading at the top of the sermon (where the leaf may have been cut), though its table of contents counts it as Clement's, that C entitles it 'Of Clement to the Corinthians', and that the Syriac calls it 'the Second Epistle' of 'the same'. Eusebius wrote: 'there is said to be a second epistle of Clement. But we do not know that this is recognized like the former, for we do not find that the ancients have made any use of it' (Church History 3.38.4). Jerome: 'There is also a second Epistle under his name which is rejected by earlier writers' (Lives of Illustrious Men 15). Lake judged that 'it cannot have been written by the author of I. Clement', and Lightfoot that its Gentile outlook and its use of the Gospel of the Egyptians set it apart from Clement's letter. The name is kept by custom.
